entry:
City (metropolitan pop., 2022: 2.4 million), capital of Mecca Province, in the [[Hejaz]] region of western [[Saudi Arabia]], and the holiest city in [[Islam]]. It lies 70 km inland from [[Jeddah]] on the Red Sea, in a narrow valley 277 m above sea level, and is the third most populated city in the country after Riyadh and Jeddah.

Mecca is regarded as the birthplace of the Prophet [[Muhammad]]. The Cave of Hira on Jabal al-Nour, just outside the city, is where Muslims believe the Quran was first revealed to him. The Great Mosque, known as the Masjid al-Haram, houses the [[Kaaba]], which Muslims believe was built by Abraham and Ishmael and which is the direction of prayer (qibla) for all Muslims worldwide. The [[Hajj]] pilgrimage, an obligation for every Muslim at least once in life, is observed in the twelfth Hijri month, Dhu al-Hijjah, and pilgrims more than triple the city's population each year. Mecca received over 19.3 million international visitors in 2024. Non-Muslims are prohibited from entering the city.

The Saudi government adopted Makkah as the official spelling in the 1980s; the name appears in the Quran (Surah Al-Fath, verse 24), as does Bakkah (Surah Al Imran, verse 96). Its etymology is obscure, and a traditional derivation is from the Old South Arabian root M-K-R-B, meaning "temple." In 2010 a fossil of *Saadanius*, a primate related to the common ancestor of the Old World monkeys and apes, was found in the area; its habitat dates to between 28 million and 29 million years ago.

Muslim rulers from in and around the region long sought to control the city, which saw several regime changes. It was most recently conquered by [[Ibn Saud]] and his allies in 1925, since when it has expanded greatly; The Clock Towers are described as the world's fourth-tallest building. The government has destroyed several historical structures and archaeological sites, such as the Ajyad Fortress, though many demolitions were officially part of expanding the Masjid al-Haram to accommodate pilgrims. Mecca is governed by the Mecca Regional Municipality, a council of 14 locally elected members headed by a mayor appointed by the Saudi government.

Engineering discipline concerned with the design, analysis, manufacture, and operation of mechanical systems. It combines engineering physics and mathematics with [[Materials science|materials science]] to develop and improve machines, structures, manufacturing processes, and fluid, thermal, and energy systems. Core areas include [[Mechanics|mechanics]], dynamics, [[Thermodynamics|thermodynamics]], design, structural analysis, electronics, and electricity. Engineers use computer-aided design (CAD), computer-aided manufacturing (CAM), computer-aided engineering (CAE), and product lifecycle management for plants, industrial equipment, heating and cooling systems, transport systems, motor vehicles, aircraft, watercraft, robotics, medical devices, and weapons.

The field emerged during the Industrial Revolution in Europe in the 18th century, but its development can be traced back several thousand years. The wedge and inclined plane were known since prehistoric times. The lever appeared around 5,000 years ago in the Near East, and the shadoof, the first crane, in Mesopotamia c. 3000 BC. Water wheels and watermills appeared in the Persian Empire by the early 4th century BC. [[Archimedes]] (287–212 BC) influenced mechanics in the Western tradition, and the geared Antikythera mechanism, an analog computer, dates to around the 2nd century BC. In China, Zhang Heng (78–139 AD) improved a water clock and invented a seismometer, and [[Su Song]] (1020–1101 AD) incorporated an escapement into his astronomical clock tower two centuries before escapements appeared in European clocks. Al-Jazari wrote his book on ingenious mechanical devices in 1206, during the Islamic Golden Age.

[[Christiaan Huygens]] invented the pendulum clock in 1657, the first reliable timekeeper for almost 300 years. [[Isaac Newton]] formulated his laws of motion and developed calculus, as did Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in the same period. In the early 19th century, machine tools developed in England, Germany, and Scotland during the [[Industrial Revolution]] allowed mechanical engineering to become a separate field, and developments in physics led to mechanical engineering science. The discipline overlaps with aerospace, civil, electrical, chemical, and industrial engineering, and with biomedical engineering through biomechanics. Engineers today pursue developments in composites, mechatronics, and nanotechnology.

Substance used to diagnose, cure, treat, or prevent disease; also called medicine, medicament, pharmaceutical drug, or simply [[Drug|drug]]. Drug therapy (pharmacotherapy) relies on [[Pharmacology|pharmacology]] for continual advancement and on [[Pharmacy|pharmacy]] for management. [[Encyclopædia Britannica|Britannica]] defines it as "a substance used in treating a disease or relieving pain." Dosage forms include tablets, capsules, liquids, creams, and patches, and routes of administration include by mouth, by infusion into a vein, and by drops in the ear or eye. A medication with no active ingredient, used in research studies, is a [[Placebo|placebo]].

Definitions vary by jurisdiction. In Europe the term is "medicinal product," defined by EU law as any substance or combination presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings, or usable to restore, correct, or modify physiological functions or to make a medical diagnosis. In the U.S., a "drug" is a substance, other than food, intended to affect the structure or any function of the body; a substance intended for the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment, or prevention of disease; or a substance recognized by an official pharmacopeia or formulary.

Drugs are classified in many ways. One key division is by level of control, separating [[Prescription drug|prescription drugs]], dispensed by a pharmacist only on prescription, from over-the-counter drugs. Another is between traditional small-molecule drugs, usually derived from chemical synthesis, and biological products such as recombinant proteins, vaccines, blood products, gene therapy, and cell therapy. Drugs may also be classified by mode of action, route of administration, biological system affected, or therapeutic effect; a widely used scheme is the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) Classification System. The [[World Health Organization]] keeps a list of essential medicines.

Historically, drugs were found by isolating active ingredients from traditional remedies or by serendipity. Since the sequencing of the human genome, high-throughput screening of large compound libraries against isolated biological targets has become common. Discovery and development are complex and expensive, and partnering is standard practice. Governments generally regulate which drugs can be marketed, how, and in some jurisdictions at what price. Controversies have arisen over drug pricing and disposal of used medications. Adverse drug reactions are a recognized risk, and polypharmacy in older adults heightens the incidence of falls and cognitive impairment.

Science and practice of caring for patients, managing the diagnosis, prognosis, prevention, treatment, and palliation of injury or disease while promoting health. It encompasses health care practices that evolved to maintain and restore health through the prevention and treatment of illness and infection. Contemporary medicine applies biomedical sciences, biomedical research, genetics, and medical technology to diagnose, treat, and prevent injury and disease, typically through pharmaceuticals or [[Surgery|surgery]], but also through therapies such as psychotherapy, external splints and traction, medical devices, biologics, and ionizing radiation. The English word derives from Latin *medicus*, "a physician."

Medicine has been practiced since prehistoric times, and for most of that time it was an art, frequently connected to the religious and philosophical beliefs of local culture. A medicine man would apply herbs and say prayers for healing; an ancient philosopher and physician would apply bloodletting according to the theory of humorism, or the four humors. Since the advent of modern science, most medicine has become a combination of art and science. [[Hippocrates]], around 460 BC, emphasized natural over supernatural causes and is associated with the Hippocratic Oath. In the 19th century, [[Louis Pasteur]]'s germ theory and [[Robert Koch]]'s postulates linking microbes to specific diseases shifted the paradigm from miasma to microbial causation. [[Alexander Fleming]] discovered penicillin in 1928, and vaccination, built on [[Edward Jenner]]'s smallpox inoculation, led to the disease's eradication by 1980.

Prescientific forms, now known as [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]] or folk medicine, remain commonly used in the absence of scientific medicine and are thus called alternative medicine. Alternative treatments outside scientific medicine with ethical, safety, and efficacy concerns are termed [[Quackery|quackery]] or are described as based on fringe science. Modern scientific medicine is highly developed in the Western world, whereas populations in parts of Africa, Oceania, Southeast Asia, and Latin America often rely more heavily on traditional medicine. Even in the developed world, evidence-based medicine is not universally applied: a 2007 survey of literature reviews found that about 49% of medical interventions lacked sufficient evidence to support either benefit or harm.

In clinical practice, physicians and mid-level practitioners such as physician assistants assess patients personally. An encounter typically begins with a review of the medical history and record, followed by a medical interview and a physical examination. The interview covers the chief complaint, history of present illness, past medical history, family history, medications and allergies, social history, and a review of systems. The examination looks for objective signs of disease, as distinct from symptoms volunteered by the patient, and rests on four actions: inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation, generally in that order. Basic devices such as the stethoscope are used, and the doctor may order medical tests, take a biopsy, prescribe drugs or other therapies, or refer the patient to a specialist. The encounter is documented in the medical record, a legal document in many jurisdictions.

Medical practice is bound by the bioethical principle of non-maleficence, historically associated with the Hippocratic Oath and its primary duty to "first, do no harm."

Practice in which an individual uses a technique or combination of techniques to train attention and awareness and to detach from "discursive, ruminating thought," aiming at a mentally clear, emotionally calm, and stable state without analyzing its effects, judging its outcomes, or forming expectations. Techniques are broadly classified as focused (concentrative) methods, which direct attention to a specific object such as the breath or a mantra, and open-monitoring methods, which include mindfulness and awareness of subjective experience in the present moment and may involve the active cultivation of wisdom.

The earliest records of meditation (*dhyana*) are found in the [[Upanishads]], and it plays a salient role in the contemplative repertoire of [[Jainism]], [[Buddhism]], [[Hinduism]], and [[Taoism]]. Meditation-like techniques are also known in [[Judaism]], [[Christianity]], and [[Islam]] in the context of remembrance of, and prayer and devotion to, God. The English word comes from Old French *meditacioun*, from Latin *meditatio*, from *meditari*, "to think, contemplate, devise, ponder." In the Catholic tradition, *meditatio* as a formal, stepwise process dates to at least the 12th-century monk Guigo II. The term was later introduced as a translation for Eastern practices called *dhyāna*, from the Sanskrit root *dhyai*.

Meditation is difficult to define because it covers a wide range of dissimilar practices in different traditions and cultures, and no definition of necessary and sufficient criteria has achieved widespread acceptance in the scientific community. A 2009 study by Bond and colleagues, a five-round Delphi study with a panel of 7 experts, identified three essential criteria: a defined technique, logic relaxation, and a self-induced state or mode.

Asian techniques have spread to other cultures and are applied in non-spiritual contexts such as business and health. Jon Kabat-Zinn developed Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction in the late 1970s to bring meditation into secular therapeutic settings. Several meta-analyses of clinical studies of mindfulness have demonstrated mental and physical health benefits. Research, initially criticized for methodological weaknesses, now commonly employs randomized controlled trials, active control groups, and stronger methodological standards, and continues to examine psychological, neurological, and cardiovascular effects. Evidence supports reductions in stress, anxiety, and symptoms of depression, though meditation can occasionally exacerbate anxiety or depression in vulnerable individuals.

Intercontinental sea between Europe, Asia, and Africa, almost completely enclosed by land: by the Levant on the east, Anatolia and Southern Europe on the north, and North Africa on the south. In the west it connects to the [[Atlantic Ocean]] through the [[Strait of Gibraltar]], only 14 km wide; in the northeast to the [[Black Sea]] through the [[Bosporus]]; and in the southeast to the [[Red Sea]] via the [[Suez Canal]].

The sea covers about 2,500,000 sq km, 0.7% of the global ocean surface, and includes fifteen marginal seas, among them the Aegean, Adriatic, Tyrrhenian, and Marmara. Its average depth is 1,500 m, and the deepest recorded point is 5,109 ± 1 m in the Calypso Deep in the Ionian Sea. It lies between latitudes 30° and 46° N and longitudes 6° W and 36° E, and its west–east length is about 4,000 km. About 5.9 million years ago it was cut off from the Atlantic and was partly or completely desiccated over some 600,000 years during the Messinian salinity crisis, before the Zanclean flood refilled it about 5.3 million years ago. Mild winter and warm summer water temperatures, with most precipitation in the cooler months, give name to the [[Mediterranean climate]].

The surrounding countries, clockwise, are Spain, France, Monaco, Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Albania, Greece, Turkey, Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine (Gaza Strip), Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco; Cyprus and Malta are island countries in the sea. Northern Cyprus, Gibraltar, and the U.K. territory of Akrotiri and Dhekelia also have coastlines. The Nile is the longest river ending in the sea, and Sicily and Sardinia are its largest islands.

The Levant was among the first regions to display permanent human habitation, as early as 12,000 BC, and Egypt, Greece, and the Fertile Crescent were among the earliest civilizations of the region. The sea was an important route for merchants, travellers, and migrants, facilitating trade, cultural exchange, colonization, and conquest. The [[Roman Empire]], which called it *Mare Nostrum* ("Our Sea"), is the only state to have controlled all of its coasts. The name *Mare Mediterrāneum*, Latin for "in the middle of land," is first attested in the 6th century, in the work of Isidore of Seville. Today the sea faces eutrophication, plastic pollution, and warming waters, and irregular crossings from North Africa to Europe have resulted in over 35,000 documented deaths since 2014.

Faculty of the mind by which data or information is encoded, stored, and retrieved when needed. It is the retention of information over time for the purpose of influencing future action. Without memory of past events, language, relationships, and personal identity could not develop. Memory loss is usually described as forgetfulness or as a disorder such as [[Amnesia|amnesia]].

Memory is often understood as an information processing system made up of a sensory processor, short-term (or working) memory, and long-term memory. The sensory processor allows information from the outside world to be sensed as chemical and physical stimuli and attended to at various levels of focus and intent. Working memory serves as an encoding and retrieval processor, and long-term memory stores information through various categorical models or systems.

Declarative, or explicit, memory is the conscious storage and recollection of data and includes semantic memory, which is encoded with specific meaning, and episodic memory, which is encoded along a spatial and temporal plane. Non-declarative, or implicit, memory is the unconscious storage and recollection of information, as in procedural memory, the slow and gradual learning of skills often without conscious attention, and priming, the subliminal arousal of specific responses from memory.

Sensory memory holds information from the senses for less than one second after an item is perceived and cannot be prolonged by rehearsal. In experiments published in 1963, George Sperling used a partial-report procedure with a grid of 12 letters to show that its capacity is approximately 12 items but that it degrades within a few hundred milliseconds. Three types exist: iconic (visual), echoic (auditory), and haptic (touch). Short-term memory allows recall for several seconds to a minute without rehearsal, with very limited capacity. Memory is better when encoding emphasizes deep aspects of a stimulus, such as meaning, than shallow ones, and when cues at recall match those present during learning.

Memory is not a perfect processor. Pain impairs it, as do reduced [[Attention|attention]] to new stimuli and physical damage to areas of the [[Brain|brain]] associated with storage, such as the [[Hippocampus|hippocampus]], which is critical for forming and consolidating explicit memories. Retrieval can also be disrupted by decay within long-term memory. The cerebellum and basal ganglia support procedural learning, and disruptions in memory networks, as in [[Alzheimer's disease]], show their vulnerability.

Behavioral or mental pattern that causes significant distress or impairment of personal functioning; also called mental illness, mental health condition, or psychiatric disability. It is characterized by a clinically significant disturbance in cognition, emotional regulation, or behavior, often in a social context. Disturbances may occur as single episodes, may be persistent, or may be relapsing–remitting, and signs and symptoms vary widely between disorders. A mental disorder is one aspect of [[Mental health|mental health]].

The causes are often unclear, and theories draw on findings from many fields. Disorders may be associated with particular regions or functions of the brain. They are usually diagnosed by a mental health professional, such as a clinical psychologist, psychiatrist, psychiatric nurse, or clinical social worker, using methods such as psychometric tests but often relying on observation and questioning, with cultural and religious beliefs and social norms taken into account. The DSM-IV (1994) described a disorder as a psychological syndrome or pattern associated with distress, disability, increased risk of death, or significant loss of autonomy, excluding normal responses such as grief and deviant behavior for political, religious, or societal reasons. In 2013 the American Psychiatric Association redefined it in the DSM-5 as "a syndrome characterized by clinically significant disturbance in an individual's cognition, emotion regulation, or behavior that reflects a dysfunction in the psychological, biological, or developmental processes underlying mental functioning." ICD-11 uses a very similar definition.

Services are usually based in [[Psychiatric hospital|psychiatric hospitals]], outpatient clinics, or the community. Common treatments are [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapy]] or psychiatric medication, along with lifestyle changes, social interventions, peer support, and self-help; in a minority of cases there is involuntary detention or treatment. Prevention programs have been shown to reduce depression.

In 2019 major depression affected about 264 million people worldwide; [[Dementia|dementia]], about 50 million; [[Bipolar disorder|bipolar disorder]], about 45 million; and [[Schizophrenia|schizophrenia]] and other psychoses, about 20 million. Neurodevelopmental disorders, including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism, and intellectual disability, begin early in development. Stigma and discrimination add to the suffering and disability, prompting social movements to increase understanding and challenge exclusion.

The biomedical framing is disputed. Critics such as Thomas Szasz have argued that many conditions are "problems in living" or value judgments rather than verifiable pathologies, and some analysts warn of overdiagnosis, particularly of depression and ADHD, while supporters of the medical model point to evidence for treatment efficacy, strongest in severe cases.

Emotional, psychological, and social [[Well-being|well-being]], influencing cognition, perception, and behavior. It affects how an individual handles stress, interpersonal relationships, and decision-making. The [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) defines it as a "state of well-being in which the individual realizes their abilities, can cope with the normal stresses of life, can work productively and fruitfully, and can contribute to their community." The Public Health Agency of Canada describes it as an individual's capacity to feel, think, and act in ways that achieve a better quality of life while respecting personal, social, and cultural boundaries.

From the perspectives of positive psychology or holism, mental health is not merely the absence of mental illness but a broader state that includes the ability to enjoy life and to balance life activities with efforts to achieve psychological resilience. Cultural differences, personal philosophy, subjective assessments, and competing professional theories all affect how it is defined. Impairment in any of its capacities is a risk factor for a [[Mental disorder|mental disorder]]. About 970 million people worldwide had a mental disorder in 2019, anxiety and depression being the most common. ICD-11 is the global diagnostic standard, and the DSM-5 is used in the United States. Lifestyle factors such as diet, exercise, stress, drug use, and social connections are associated with mental health. Digital technology also affects it: constant online connection can increase stress, cyberbullying has been linked to depression and anxiety, and digital tools may expand access to support.

In the mid-19th century William Sweetser coined the term mental hygiene, which Isaac Ray defined as "the art of preserving the mind against all incidents and influences calculated to deteriorate its qualities, impair its energies, or derange its movements." In the U.S., mentally ill people had long been thought to be religiously punished and were confined inhumanely. Dorothea Dix exposed sub-standard conditions and, from 1840 to 1880, won federal support for over 30 state [[Psychiatric hospital|psychiatric hospitals]], which were nevertheless understaffed, under-resourced, and accused of violating human rights. Emil Kraepelin developed a [[Taxonomy|taxonomy]] of mental disorders in 1896 that dominated the field for nearly 80 years. Clifford Beers, after publishing *A Mind That Found Itself* (1908), founded what became Mental Health America and opened the first outpatient mental health clinic in the U.S. The mental hygiene movement was at times associated with advocating [[Eugenics|eugenics]] and the sterilization of those considered too mentally deficient to work. After World War II the term "mental health" gradually replaced mental hygiene, shifting emphasis from treating illness to prevention and promotion.

Access to care remains uneven: the WHO African Region averages 2.2 mental health workers per 100,000 population against a global median of 13.5. Critics argue that diagnostic expansion has led to overmedicalization.

Innermost and smallest planet of the [[Solar System]], first from the [[Sun]]. It is a rocky [[Terrestrial planet|terrestrial planet]] with a trace atmosphere and a surface gravity slightly lower than that of Mars. Its cratered surface resembles that of the Moon, with an expansive system of scarps formed by thrust faults and bright ray systems formed by ejecta. The largest crater, Caloris Planitia, is 1,550 km across, about one-third the planet's diameter of 4,880 km. Its equatorial radius is 2,439.7 km, and it is smaller, though more massive, than Ganymede and Titan. Because it orbits closest to the Sun, it always appears near the Sun in Earth's sky, as a "morning star" or an "evening star."

Mercury's sidereal year (88.0 Earth days) and sidereal day (58.65 Earth days) are in a 3:2 spin–orbit resonance, so one solar day, from sunrise to sunrise, lasts around 176 Earth days. A tenuous exosphere and a faint magnetic field, just strong enough to deflect the solar wind, surround the planet. Equatorial temperatures range from −170 °C at night to 420 °C in sunlight, making it the second hottest planet after [[Venus]], since it lacks an atmosphere to trap heat. Its very small axial tilt leaves the poles permanently shadowed, which strongly suggests that water ice may be present in the craters.

The planet is about 70% metallic and 30% silicate material. Its density, 5.427 g/cm³, is the second highest in the Solar System, only slightly less than Earth's, implying a large iron-rich core. Current models describe a solid silicate crust and mantle over a solid outer core layer, a deeper liquid core layer, and a solid inner core. The core radius is estimated at 2,020 ± 30 km and occupies about 57% of the volume, against 17% for Earth. Mercury formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago, and hypotheses about its origin remain competing. It is expected to be destroyed when the Sun becomes a red giant in approximately seven or eight billion years.

The ancient Greeks had realized by about 350 BC that the morning and evening "stars" were the same body. The Romans named it after the swift messenger god Mercurius, equated with the Greek Hermes. Mariner 10 made the first successful flyby in 1974, and the planet has since been explored by the MESSENGER and BepiColombo orbiters.
